title: Satie's Vexations
hook: A one-page piano piece that, played as marked, lasts most of a day.
peek: Erik Satie wrote a short, strange piano piece with a note suggesting it be played 840 times. In 1963 John Cage organised a relay of pianists in New York who did exactly that. It took about 18 hours.
lede: Around 1893, Erik Satie wrote Vexations: a slow, unsettled theme that fits on a single page and lasts a minute or two. Above it he left a cryptic note. It says that to play this motif 840 times in a row, one should prepare in deep silence. Nobody knows whether Satie meant it seriously, but in 1963 a group of musicians decided to find out.

bullets.text: Some scholars read the note as a real performance direction, others as one of Satie's dry jokes. The piece was not published in his lifetime and only became widely known decades later.
John Cage organised the first complete performance at the Pocket Theatre in New York. A team of pianists took turns at the keyboard in shifts, and the piece ran for roughly 18 hours.
The team included Cage himself, the pianist David Tudor and a young John Cale, who later co-founded the Velvet Underground. A careful tally of repetitions made sure the total reached 840.
The piece now draws regular marathon concerts, sometimes by one pianist alone. Players describe the strange way the music seems to change in the mind even though not a note of it does.
